Converting low-quality library scans into large-print editions with layout analysis and constraint-based reflow⋆
SCIA-2026: International Workshop on Social Communication and Information Activity in Digital Humanities, December 10, 2026, Lviv, Ukraine
Rostyslav Zatserkovnyi1,∗,†, Roksoliana Zatserkovna2,†
1 Lviv University of Trade and Economics, 10 Tuhan-Baranovskyi Str., Lviv, 79008, Ukraine
2 Lviv Polytechnic National University, 12 Stepan Bandera Str., Lviv, 79013, Ukraine
Abstract

Public-domain scans in library repositories are normally published together with the OCR derivative that the repository's own pipeline produced, and that derivative is the cheapest route to a reflowable large-print edition for readers with low vision. It is also the riskiest: the derivatives were made by different engines over two decades, their word-level confidence values are not comparable between volumes, and reflowing them faithfully reproduces every recognition error at 18 pt. We describe a pipeline that decides, passage by passage, whether the recognised text is trustworthy enough to reflow, and keeps the remainder as magnified, deskewed images of the original lines, re-imposed to fit the new measure. Layout analysis strips running heads and folios and recovers headings and verse; a calibrated reliability model estimates the probability that each recognised token is wrong; a budgeted selection withdraws the least trustworthy passages from the reflowable layer; and a dynamic program paginates the mixed material under typographic constraints. On 14 public-domain volumes (4,834 scanned pages, 1.19 million words aligned to clean e-texts as reference transcriptions), the reliability model ranks erroneous tokens better than the engines' own confidence in every volume (mean AUC 0.845 against 0.719). Withdrawing 10% of the running text removes 28.4% of the errors a reader would otherwise meet, against 23.6% for confidence-based selection, at no cost in pages. Constrained pagination removes 99.5% of widows, orphans and stranded headings for 1.4% more pages.
Keywords

large-print editions, low vision accessibility, document layout analysis, text reflow, OCR quality 1

Library digitisation programmes have put tens of millions of scanned volumes within reach of anyone with a network connection. For a reader with low vision, however, a scanned page is not yet a readable book. The page image carries the type size of the original edition, and nineteenth-century trade printing is small relative to its page: shown whole on A4, only 14% of the pages in our corpus reach 18 pt, the size at which large print is usually said to begin. Enlarging the image is possible in any viewer, but a page magnified to a comfortable size no longer fits the display, and the reader is left panning line by line. What is wanted instead is a genuine large-print edition: the same text, reset at 18 pt or more, on pages that can be read straight through.

The material for such a reset edition is already there. Repositories publish, beside each scan, the output of their own optical character recognition, with word rectangles and per-word confidence, in the hOCR microformat [1] or a comparable schema [2]. Reflowing that text is cheap and produces output that is not merely larger but genuinely accessible: it can be resized further by the reader, read aloud by a screen reader, searched, and re-rendered on a phone. The difficulty is that the recognised text is wrong often enough to matter. Across our corpus 3.30% of recognised words differ from the reference transcription, and in the worst volume the figure is 9.8%. A reader of a facsimile meets the printer's text; a reader of an uncorrected reflow meets the recogniser's, with no way of telling which is which.

This paper takes that tension as a design problem rather than a recognition problem. Instead of trying to correct the text, we decide where to trust it. Passages the system judges reliable are reflowed as real text at the target size. Passages it does not trust are kept as images of the original lines, magnified to the same target size and re-imposed so that each line still fits the new measure. The output is one document in which most of the content is reflowable and the rest is a faithful magnified facsimile, and in which the reader is never shown a confidently typeset misreading.

The contributions are as follows. First, we show that the confidence values libraries publish with their OCR are not usable as a trust signal across a collection, because different engines and different vintages of the same engine put them on different scales, and we give a calibrated replacement built from engine-agnostic features that transfers to unseen volumes. Second, we formulate the choice between reflowed text and magnified facsimile as a selection under an explicit coverage budget, which gives a librarian a single dial between reflowability and residual error rather than an opaque threshold. Third, we compose the mixed material with optimal ragged-right line breaking and a pagination dynamic program that treats widows, orphans and stranded headings as hard constraints. Fourth, we report a reproducible evaluation on 14 public-domain volumes from the Internet Archive, using clean Project Gutenberg e-texts of the same works as reference transcriptions, and we measure our own layout analysis honestly enough to change the design where it proved unreliable.

That mass-digitised text is noisy, and that the noise propagates, is well established. Traub et al. [3] quantified how recognition quality changes the outcome of archival search tasks; Hill and Hengchen [4] showed that quantitative analyses of an eighteenth-century corpus shift measurably when run on dirty text; van Strien et al. [5] traced the effect through a series of language-processing tasks. Cordell [6] argues that recognition output should be read as a historical artefact in its own right rather than as a transparent window onto the page. The standard response is post-correction, surveyed by Nguyen et al. [7] and benchmarked by the ICDAR competition series [8, 9]; a research agenda for the area is set out by Smith and Cordell [10]. Post-correction and the present work are complementary: correction reduces the error rate of the text layer, and what we do is decide how much of the remaining error a reader should be exposed to.

Document layout analysis is a mature field with comprehensive surveys [11], standard ground-truth formats [2] and datasets [12], and modern learned toolkits [13]. Detecting recurring page apparatus such as running heads is related to the structural tasks studied for tables of contents [14]. Reflowing a scanned page onto a small display was studied two decades ago under the heading of document image reflow: the Paper-to-PDA line of work [15] segmented the page into line images and re-laid them out at a size suited to a handheld screen. Our re-imposition step is a descendant of that idea, applied for a different reason – not a small screen but a large type size – and mixed with reflowed text rather than used alone. The composition machinery is classical: optimal line breaking follows Knuth and Plass [16], and page breaking follows the dynamic-programming formulations of complex-document pagination [17].

Vision science gives the target a precise meaning. Legge and Bigelow [18] review the relation between print size and reading speed and locate the fluent range well above the sizes used in trade printing. Studies of typeface legibility for readers with low vision [19, 20] and of type size for older readers [21] support the practical guidance that large print begins at about 18 pt, that generous leading and a moderate measure help, and that justified setting and hyphenation hinder. Letter spacing matters as well [22]. Accessibility standards approach the same target from the digital side: WCAG 2.2 [23] requires text to be resizable and reflowable, EPUB Accessibility 1.1 [24] sets conformance requirements for digital publications, and the European Accessibility Act [25] makes such requirements binding for e-books placed on the Union market from 2025. The Marrakesh Treaty [26] gives authorised entities the right to make accessible-format copies of published works, which is precisely the activity this pipeline is meant to support. Production tooling for print-disabled readers has been studied mostly at the level of the individual edition, for instance by modelling the quality of adapted textbooks for readers with low vision [27]; producing large-print editions at the scale of a digitised collection has received less attention, although it would serve a far larger population.

We fix the output format before describing the method, because the format determines what the layout engine has to achieve. Pages are A4 with 20 mm margins, giving a measure of 482 pt. Running text is set at 18 pt with 1.4 line spacing in Atkinson Hyperlegible, a typeface designed for readers with low vision. Setting is ragged right rather than justified, and hyphenation is disabled, both following the guidance summarised above. Captions and notes are set at the same size as the body. Headings are 22 pt. Composed body lines average 57 characters, which is inside the range usually recommended for large print.

Two properties of the output are treated as non-negotiable. The first is typographic: no paragraph may be split so that a single line stands alone at the foot or the head of a page, and no heading may be separated from the text it introduces. A reader who has to work to follow the thread of a page is poorly served by a format whose whole purpose is to reduce effort. The second is that page apparatus belongs to the original page, not to the work: running heads, folios and catchwords must not be scattered through the reset text.

The input to the pipeline is what a repository publishes: a page image per leaf and an hOCR file giving, for every page, a hierarchy of regions, paragraphs, lines and words, each with a bounding rectangle, and for every word a confidence value and an estimated type size [1]. No re-recognition is performed. This is deliberate: the derivatives already exist for millions of volumes, and a method that needs only them can be run over a collection at negligible cost.

Paragraphs are placed in reading order, with a projection over paragraph centres used to detect two-column pages, and are then assigned a role. Page apparatus is found by a whole-page test: the single-line paragraph at the very top or the very bottom of a page is furniture if its opening words recur across the volume, or if it consists only of a page number. Keying the recurrence test on the opening words rather than the whole line matters, because the tail of a running head is often the part the recogniser garbles, and a key built from the whole line differs on every page.

Headings are recognised from type size, capitalisation and brevity. Verse needs a whole-page test of its own, because recognisers emit one paragraph per verse line and a paragraph-local rule cannot see a stanza: a page is verse when most of its lines stop well short of the right margin, its paragraphs are one or two lines long, a short line is not followed by an indented one, and the short lines do not begin with quotation marks. The last condition separates verse from rapid dialogue, which otherwise produces the same geometric signature. Verse paragraphs keep their original line division in the output instead of being reflowed, with a run-over indent where a verse line is too long for the new measure.

Every recognised token receives an estimate of the probability that it differs from what is printed. The features fall into four groups. Lexical features record whether the normalised token, or a light morphological variant of it, appears in a period lexicon built from Webster's 1913 Unabridged and from clean e-texts disjoint from the evaluation corpus. Shape features record length, the proportion of non-alphanumeric characters, runs of punctuation, case transitions inside a word, and isolated one- or two-letter tokens that are not English short words. Geometric features record how far the line's type size and the token's height and aspect depart from the volume's median, and the token's vertical position on the page. Confidence features use the engine's value, but in three forms: the raw value, its z-score within the volume, and its rank percentile within the volume. Two neighbourhood features average the confidence percentile and lexicon membership of the surrounding tokens, which captures the tendency of recognition failures to cluster.

A logistic model over these features is fitted and evaluated leave-one-volume-out, so that every reported number describes transfer to a volume the model has never seen. Within-volume normalisation is the component that makes transfer possible: the raw confidence scales differ so sharply between derivatives that a threshold tuned on one volume is meaningless on another. Calibration is assessed with the expected calibration error, in the manner usual for probability estimates [28, 29], because the routing stage consumes probabilities rather than ranks.

Let a segment be a paragraph, with n tokens and estimated expected error e. Routing chooses, for each segment, whether it is reflowed as text or kept as facsimile. Keeping a segment as facsimile removes its expected errors from the text layer, but also removes its words from the reflowable, screen-readable part of the edition. We therefore make reflowable coverage the budgeted resource: the operator specifies the fraction of running words that may be withdrawn, and the system withdraws segments in decreasing order of estimated error density until the budget is spent. This is the fractional-knapsack ordering and is optimal for the relaxed problem; with paragraph-sized items the integrality gap is negligible.

Expressing the control as a coverage budget rather than a confidence threshold has a practical benefit beyond optimality. A threshold on a confidence value means something different in every volume, as Section 6.3 shows; a coverage budget means the same thing everywhere, and it lets us compare selection rules at matched coverage, which is how the experiments below are organised.

Text segments are broken into lines by a Knuth–Plass dynamic program [16] in its ragged-right form: interword space is fixed, and the badness of a line is a cubic function of how far short of the measure it stops, so the optimisation evens out the right-hand edge instead of stretching word spaces. Hyphenation is disabled, and the last line of a paragraph is free.

Pagination is a second dynamic program over the resulting stream of atomic items – text lines, facsimile strips and illustrations. The cost of a page is a constant plus a penalty for unused height, so that minimising cost minimises the page count and then prefers full pages. Breaks that would leave a paragraph's opening line alone at the foot of a page, carry its closing line alone to the next, strand a heading at a page foot, or separate a heading from the first two lines it introduces are charged a penalty large enough to act as a hard constraint. Because the constraint is expressed in the objective rather than as a filter, the program still returns a layout when a segment is physically too tall to satisfy it.

A segment routed to facsimile is not pasted in as a block. Each source line is cut out separately and scaled so that its type reaches the target size; since the hOCR type size is reported in scan pixels, the scale factor for a line is simply the ratio of the target size to the reported size, and the strip's height in points follows from its rectangle. A strip wider than the measure is divided at an interword gap – the word rectangles give the gaps directly – and continued on the next strip with a run-over indent. Strips are atomic items for the pagination program, so a facsimile passage flows across a page break exactly as reflowed text does.

Scans of bound volumes, and microfilm in particular, are rarely square to the page, and a rectangular crop of a sloping line catches the descenders of its neighbours. The baseline slope that the recogniser already reports for each line is used to rotate each strip upright before it is placed, which removes the artefact without any image analysis of our own. One further practical detail is that the order of pages in a published hOCR file does not always agree with the repository's own leaf numbering; the offset is recovered automatically by matching the aspect ratio of a few sample leaves against the page rectangles in the hOCR.

The corpus is 14 public-domain volumes from the Internet Archive, listed in Table 1, chosen so that each work also exists as a clean Project Gutenberg e-text and so that the set spans prose, illustrated prose and verse, printings from 1851 to 1902, and three different recognition engines. One volume is a microfilm-derived scan, included deliberately as a worst-case source. Together the volumes comprise 4,834 scanned pages, 1,226,199 recognised tokens and 1,136 illustration regions.

The corpus. Word error is measured against the Project Gutenberg e-text of the same work, over the scorable tokens only.

The e-text of the same work supplies the reference transcription. Aligning the two word streams labels every recognised token as correct, substituted or spurious. Alignment follows the anchor-based scheme used for automatic evaluation of book recognition [30, 31]: five-gram sequences that occur exactly once in each stream are matched, a longest increasing subsequence gives a monotone chain of anchors, and the gaps between consecutive anchors are aligned with a sequence matcher. Line-final hyphens are joined before alignment, so that a word broken across two lines is compared as one word.

Scanned volumes and e-texts do not agree on everything: a scan carries front matter, plates, advertisements and an editor's introduction that the e-text does not, and the two may represent different editions. A token is therefore scored only when it falls inside a gap between anchors that is short and of comparable length on both sides; long or lopsided gaps mean divergent content rather than recognition error and are left unscored. 97.0% of tokens are scorable under this rule, and the pooled word error over them is 3.30% (95% CI 3.27–3.33%), computed with the Wilson interval [32, 33] as all proportions in this paper are.

Three quantities describe an edition. Residual error density is the number of erroneous recognised words that the edition presents as text, per thousand scorable words of the work; an all-facsimile edition scores zero by construction. Reflowable coverage is the fraction of running words delivered as text rather than as images, and stands for everything a text layer buys the reader: further magnification, screen reading, search, re-rendering. Extent is the number of A4 pages. We also report typographic violations per hundred pages and the root-mean-square raggedness of the right-hand edge over body lines.

Five composition strategies are compared at full coverage. Magnify-and-tile crops each scanned page to its text block, magnifies it until the type reaches 18 pt and tiles the result across A4 pages; this is the baseline a page-image viewer effectively offers, and it is given every advantage. All-facsimile re-imposes every line as a magnified strip. Greedy-reflow sets all recognised text with first-fit line breaking and fills pages to capacity. Unconstrained Knuth–Plass replaces the line breaker only. Constrained reflow adds the pagination program.

Four selection rules are then compared at matched coverage budgets of 2, 5, 10, 20 and 40%. All four withdraw segments through the same procedure and differ only in how they rank them: by the reliability model's mean predicted error probability; by the engine's own mean confidence, which is the obvious alternative; at random, which is the floor; and by the true error density measured against the reference transcription, which is the ceiling attainable by any ranking.

Showing a scanned page whole on A4 reaches 18 pt on only 14% of the pages in the corpus. Cropping away the original margins first is much more effective and gets 78% of pages there, but the remainder is concentrated: in three volumes fewer than one page in ten reaches the target even after cropping. Tiling the magnified pages so that the target size is always met costs 9,286 pages, 1.65 times the extent of a reflowed edition of the same content and 1.92 times the extent of the original volumes. Magnification alone is thus neither compact nor uniformly sufficient, quite apart from producing nothing a screen reader can use.

Removal of page apparatus can be checked without hand labelling, because running heads, folios and catchwords are printing apparatus that does not appear in the e-text of the work. Aligning the unfiltered token stream against the e-text shows that of the 14,697 tokens the analysis calls furniture, only 1.1% match the reference transcription (95% CI 1.0–1.3%), while 94.4% of the tokens it keeps as body text do. In other words the filter discards almost nothing that belongs to the work.

The finer roles are less trustworthy. Table 2 reports precision on a sample of twelve paragraphs per predicted class, drawn across all volumes and adjudicated by the authors against the scanned pages. Furniture and verse are reliable; heading detection confuses chapter titles with the running heads that escaped the furniture filter; and caption and footnote detection are poor, because the illustration regions the recognisers emit are over-generated and body text often sits next to one. That tokens labelled caption match the e-text almost as often as body text does (Table 2) corroborates the sampled verdict that most of them are body text. Because the sample is stratified by predicted class it measures per-class precision, not overall accuracy; furniture and body together account for 97% of all tokens.

This measurement changed the design. An earlier version of the system set captions and footnotes two points smaller than the body, as a printed book would. Given the measured precision, that decision would have set misclassified body text below the large-print threshold on a non-trivial number of paragraphs, so captions and notes are now set at the body size and the caption and footnote labels are used only for ordering. The composition rules rely only on the distinctions the analysis gets right.
Table 2

Layout analysis. Precision is adjudicated on twelve sampled paragraphs per predicted class. The last two columns give, for all tokens of that class, how often they match the reference transcription; apparatus is expected not to match, running text is.

The confidence values published with the derivatives are not comparable across the collection. In one volume no token is assigned a confidence above 30 and the modal value is 29; in another, produced by a recent Tesseract release, 93% of tokens score 90 or more. Pooled over the corpus, ranking tokens by raw confidence gives an AUC of 0.683 for the task of finding the erroneous ones, and replacing the raw value by its rank percentile within the volume raises this only to 0.715: the problem is not merely one of scale.

The full model, evaluated leave-one-volume-out, reaches a mean AUC of 0.845 (SD 0.077) against 0.719 (SD 0.112) for raw confidence, and is better on all 14 volumes (sign test, p = 1.2 × 10−4). Figure 2 shows the per-volume comparison. The margin is largest exactly where it is most useful: on volumes whose confidence values carry almost no signal, such as Walden (AUC 0.598 from confidence, 0.857 from the model) and Moby-Dick (0.618 against 0.798). The hardest volume for both is The Time Machine, which has the highest error rate in the corpus and the least informative confidence values. Mean expected calibration error is 0.018; Figure 3 shows the pooled reliability diagram, which tracks the diagonal across two orders of magnitude with a mild tendency to over-predict at the low end and under-predict at the high end.

Table 3 gives the composition strategies at full coverage. Greedy line breaking and Knuth–Plass produce the same number of pages, which is expected when hyphenation is disabled and paragraphs are long; the difference is in the right-hand edge, whose root-mean-square raggedness falls from 0.0703 to 0.0663, a reduction of 5.7%. The pagination program is where the substantive difference lies: it removes 99.5% of widows, orphans and stranded headings, from 1,842 occurrences to 10, at a cost of 1.4% more pages. No widows and no orphans survive; the residual 10 are all stranded headings on display pages – title pages, half-titles and publishers' advertisements – where every line is classified as a heading and there is no following body text for the keep-with-next rule to attach to. All-facsimile costs 6.7% more pages than constrained reflow, which is the price of carrying line images rather than reset type.

Table 4 and Figure 4 give the central result. Reflowing everything exposes 33.0 erroneous words per thousand. Withdrawing 10% of the running text on the reliability model's ranking brings this to 23.6, a reduction of 28.4%, and closes 64% of the gap between reflowing everything and the best any ranking could do. The same budget spent on the engine's confidence reaches only 25.2, a reduction of 23.6%, and spent at random 29.6. At a 40% budget the model reaches 11.7 against 14.1 for confidence and 19.7 for random, with the oracle at 5.3.

The page cost of this is small and, at moderate budgets, negative. At a 10% budget the edition is 0.3% shorter than the all-text edition: the total vertical extent of the content falls by 0.26%, because in most volumes a magnified image of a short source line occupies slightly less height than the same words reflowed with their own line spacing. Only at a 40% budget does the extent rise, by 2.2%. The operator is therefore trading reflowability against residual error, not pages against error, which is the honest way to present the choice.

Per volume (Table 5) the reliability model beats the confidence ranking in 10 of the 14 volumes at the 10% operating point; the paired sign test over volumes is not significant (p = 0.18), although the pooled difference is decisive, the Wilson intervals 23.4–23.9 and 25.0–25.5 being disjoint. The four exceptions are informative. A Christmas Carol is the smallest volume in the corpus (10,891 scorable tokens) and the only one in which random withdrawal beats both rankings, which is what one expects when the error is spread evenly rather than concentrated. Leaves of Grass and Tom Sawyer are the two volumes in which paragraph segmentation is weakest – free verse in the first, dialogue in the second – so paragraph-level ranking has less to work with; in Dracula the two rankings are level to within 0.1 per thousand. The microfilm volume is the clearest win (24.0 to 12.7 against 16.3), but also the one case where the page cost is real: its line rectangles are tall relative to the type, so its facsimile strips are expensive, and the extent grows by 17%.

Figure 5 shows one page of the microfilm volume beside the page of the large-print edition that carries the same text. The running head and the folio have gone; three paragraphs are reflowed at 18 pt; and two passages that the reliability model distrusted are kept as magnified, deskewed strips of the original setting, each fitted to the new measure. A reader meets the printer's letterforms exactly where the recogniser was least trustworthy, and reset type everywhere else.

The result that matters practically is that the confidence values libraries publish are not, by themselves, a usable trust signal across a collection, and that a small model over features any consumer of hOCR already has does much better and transfers to unseen volumes. This is a modest claim technically and a consequential one operationally: a production pipeline that thresholds on published confidence will behave differently on every volume it meets, in ways its operators cannot see.

Several limitations bound the evidence. The corpus is English-language literary prose and verse from a single repository; scholarly editions with dense apparatus, newspapers, and non-Latin scripts are untested, and the lexical features in particular would need rebuilding for another language. Reference transcriptions come from e-texts of the same work rather than of the same printing, which is why a tenth of tokens is left unscored; the unscored material is front matter and divergent editions, which is precisely the material a large-print edition would also contain, so the reported error rates describe the alignable body of the work rather than the whole volume. Reflowable coverage is a proxy for accessibility value and weights all words equally, whereas a reader would rather lose a page of advertisements than a page of the novel. Most importantly, no reader has yet been involved: the case that the hybrid output is preferable to either extreme rests on the argument that exposed recognition errors are harmful and reflowability is valuable, not on measured reading performance. A study with low-vision readers, measuring reading speed and comprehension across the operating curve, is the natural next step and would also give the coverage budget an empirical setting rather than an operator's guess; instruments for assessing how usable an adapted edition is to such readers already exist [34] and could be applied at several points along the curve.

Two engineering limitations are worth naming. Facsimile strips are images and carry no text layer, so the passages the system distrusts are also the passages a screen reader cannot voice; attaching the low-confidence recognised text to the strip as alternative text would recover that at the cost of reintroducing the error into the speech channel, and the right trade-off there is not obvious. And the layout analysis is rule-based; a learned segmenter [13] would very likely repair the caption and footnote classes that we measured and then chose not to rely on. A third is that the type size a derivative reports for a line is engine-dependent and is not always a font size, so the magnification applied to a facsimile strip reaches the target only approximately; a measurement of x-height on the page image itself would make the target exact at the cost of touching the image.

Large-print editions of digitised books can be produced from the recognition derivatives libraries already publish, without re-recognising anything and without asking a reader to choose between a faithful facsimile they must pan across and a reflowable text full of invisible errors. The pipeline described here decides passage by passage which of the two to use, controls that decision with a coverage budget that means the same thing in every volume, and composes the mixed material under typographic constraints that a reader with low vision has good reason to expect. On 14 volumes, withdrawing a tenth of the running text removes 28.4% of the errors a reader would otherwise meet, at no cost in pages.
